chunks: From him, from Faḍālah, from Muʿāwiyah ibn ʿAmmār, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:

I asked him about a man who had offered a sacrificial animal and it became injured. He said: If it was guaranteed, then a replacement is upon him; and what is guaranteed is that which was for a vow, or an expiation, or an oath. And he may eat from it. But if it was not guaranteed, then nothing is upon him.

His statement عليه السلام, “And he may eat from it,” is understood to mean when it is voluntary and not when it is obligatory, because that which is obligatory is not permissible for him to eat from. That is indicated by what follows.

key_terms.جَزَاءً: an offering due as compensation or expiation
key_terms.مَضْمُونَةً: legally guaranteed and therefore requiring replacement if lost or damaged
key_terms.نَذْرًا: an offering made obligatory through a vow
key_terms.هَدْيًا: a sacrificial offering sent for hajj rites
key_terms.يَمِينًا: an offering connected to an oath-based obligation

ai.seo_question: If a hady animal is damaged before reaching its place, must it be replaced?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a legal ruling concerning a sacrificial offering that is damaged before reaching its destination. If the offering was obligatory—such as one due to a vow, expiation, or oath—a replacement is required; if it was not obligatory, nothing is due. The statement about eating from it is understood in the case of a voluntary offering.
